messages.subject: trying to understand reactivity
parts:
I am still trying to get a handle on how reactive programming works. Particularly when a reactive function is linked to a tab not shown immediately in an app. The gist link below has the code example I have been working on to illustrate my confusion.

In non-reactive R functions call each other. In reactive they keep track of each other and change and updated 'when-needed'. It is the when-needed part that is less clear. If Shiny picks up the right dependencies, great. If not, for what ever reason, what is the best way to suggest the appropriate dependencies?

In my example gist, if a dataframe is changed in the data2 function the list of variable names is changed (although *not* if varnames() is reactive for some reason) and the correct data is displayed (i.e., the first column has been dropped). As far as I can see from using options(shiny.trace=TRUE) the data1 and its function are not called again to show the updated version of the data (in the Data1 tab) but rather a cached version is used. 

Again, if Shiny picks up the right dependencies, great. If not what is the best way to suggest the appropriate dependencies? Also, what is the best way to visualize what reactive link are being used?

I have been stuck on this issue for some time now and could really use some help. Thanks.

https://gist.github.com/4436647

Joe: I saw your comment in my earlier post. I wanted to redo the gist and post so I deleted that one. The commented code wasn't the issue but thanks for checking :)

messages.author: 55771919c42cb6a1
messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
parts:
If you call a reactive function and then call it again without changing any of the inputs, then it uses a cached copy of the output, as you found. Shiny should always pick up the correct dependencies; if it fails to do so, then that's buggy behavior. 

As for visualizing the reactive dependencies, right now there isn't an easy way to do that, sorry! One of the things we want to do in the future is develop a tool for generating visualizations for this.

-Winston

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
parts:
Hi Vincent,

It looks like you're currently trying to get the changedata function to run and mutate input$dataset so all the other readers of input$dataset see the changed value. Instead of a function that *updates* the data, I would go with a reactive function that *wraps* the data:

mydata <- reactive(function() {
  data <- get(input$dataset)
  data[,1] <- NULL
  data
})

Now, everything else in the gist that currently calls get(input$dataset) to get the data, should instead call mydata().

In general, if you care about non-reactive side effects (such as assign(input$dataset, ...)) then you should not be using a reactive function. Instead you should be using an observer (see ?observe), or better yet, eliminate the non-reactive side effects altogether (as the above).

Reactive function is really a misnomer. We should've called them reactive expressions. If you have a reactive function "foo", then calling foo() does not mean "execute the function". Instead it means, "give me the current value of foo and let me know if it ever becomes out of date". It's possible that calling foo() will result in the actual code of the function executing right then; it's equally possible that it won't.

I have to apologize again that we don't have this better documented. Our docs up until now have been designed for people who are just getting started and for whom this level of understanding of reactivity isn't necessary. You and the other more advanced members of the Shiny community have gotten more deep into this stuff than we were really prepared for, and we recognize that we need the docs and other resources to catch up to the community.

So let's make sure I understand you right.

1) The actual underlying data never changes.
2) Sometimes you want to add residuals or whatever.
3) Probably you don't want to calculate the residuals when they won't need to be displayed.
4) The residuals are expensive to calculate so once you calculate them, you'd like to keep them around and reuse them (unless something changes about the underlying data changes, if assumption #1 is incorrect; then they need to be recalculated when needed).

messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
parts:
OK I finally understood what you were trying to do with respect to modifying the dataset. I just sent you a pull request: https://github.com/mostly-harmless/damshiny/pull/1

The key here is that when you modify a value that is depended on by other reactive functions (in this case, the dataset) you need to make sure that both reads and writes happen in a way that the reactive system can be aware that something has happened. Regular gets/assign/<- do not meet those criteria.

On master, we've introduced a new feature called reactive values. You use the reactiveValue function to create them. They behave sort of like when you read input$foo; whenever input$foo changes in the future, any reactive functions will know they are out of date. In the same way, when you read a reactive value, when that reactive value changes in the future you'll be notified. However, the difference is that you can write reactive values as well. This is what you were asking for further back in this(?) thread but I didn't think it's what you actually needed at the time.

Create reactive values like this:

  foo <- reactiveValue(100) # initial value of 100

Read them like this:

  value(foo)

Write them like this:

  value(foo) <- 200

In your particular case, you have multiple datasets that you want to reference dynamically (i.e. not hard coding the name), so I created an environment to hold them. Another solution in the future will be to use a Values object, which looks sort of like an environment (or dictionary/hashtable in other languages) but is reactive-aware:

datasets <- shiny:::Values$new()
datasets$set("mtcars", mtcars)
isolate({
  print(datasets$get("mtcars"))
})

Values' set/get operations are reactive-aware, and they are implemented slightly more efficiently than what I did in your pull request. Also it has the advantage that if you call Values$get with a name that doesn't exist in the list yet, then if it's later added, you'll be notified (and vice versa--if you get a value that is later removed, you will also be notified).

This is probably a lot to digest already--I've leave it there.

parts:
Values has been there since day 1, it's just not exported. So you can use it today by saying shiny:::Values$new() instead of just Values$new(). The downside of this is that we could rename it (and probably will, to something more descriptive like ReactiveValues) at any time since it's not part of the public API.

To set something into an environment, use assign(name, value, pos=datasetEnv). So in this case,
  assign(file, reactiveValue(read.csv(...)), pos=datasetEnv)

Then read it with
  value(get(file, pos=datasetEnv))

and modify it with
  value(get(file, pos=datasetEnv)) <- newvalues
